scope.summary: The `retry` helper that re-runs a flaky call with exponential backoff.

sections.title: What retry is for
sections.body:
`retry` wraps a call that can fail for a moment, such as a network request, and runs it again instead of failing the whole operation.

It only retries `TransientError`. Any other exception means the call is wrong, not unlucky, so it propagates at once.

terms.definition: The one error class that means try again.
How many times `call` runs at most, the first run included.
The wait function, `time.sleep` unless a caller passes another.

checkpoints.prompt: `call` raises `KeyError` on its first run. What does `retry` do?

options.why: Only `TransientError` is caught, so every other exception leaves the loop on the first attempt.

options.text: Retries up to `attempts` times, then raises.
options.why: Misconception: retry catches every exception. The `except` clause names one class.
Misconception: a caught error is swallowed. Nothing here returns without a successful `call()`.

checkpoints.explanation: The `except TransientError` clause is the filter: a bug in `call` should fail fast rather than be retried.

checkpoints.prompt: Why is `sleep` a parameter instead of calling `time.sleep` directly? Pick every reason that applies.

options.text: A test can pass a fake and run without waiting.
options.why: Injecting the clock is what lets a test assert the delays in milliseconds.

options.text: A caller in an async context can pass its own sleep function.
options.why: Any callable with the same shape fits, so the helper is not tied to one way of waiting.
Misconception: injection changes speed. The default is still `time.sleep`.

sections.title: The loop and the backoff
sections.body:
Each pass of the loop is one attempt. A successful `call()` returns straight out of the loop.

A `TransientError` waits `base_delay * 2 ** attempt` seconds and tries again, so the waits double: 0.5, 1, 2, and so on. The last attempt does not wait. It re-raises the error for the caller.

elements.mermaid:
flowchart TD
  begin([attempt n]) -->|runs| run[call]
  run -->|returns| done([value to caller])
  run -->|raises other error| out([propagates at once])
  run -->|raises TransientError| last{last attempt?}
  last -->|yes| reraise([re-raise to caller])
  last -->|no| wait[sleep base_delay times 2 to the n]
  wait -->|next n| begin
elements.caption: Only `TransientError` loops back, and only while attempts are left. Every other exit leaves the loop at once.

checkpoints.prompt: Which line hands the final failure back to the caller?
checkpoints.explanation: The bare `raise` on line 7 re-raises the caught `TransientError` once no attempts are left.

checkpoints.prompt: `call` always raises `TransientError`. What does this print?
checkpoints.explanation: Four attempts leave three gaps between them, doubling from 1. The last attempt re-raises without sleeping.

final.prompt: Put the events of a call that fails once, then succeeds, in order.
Complete the delay so the waits double on every attempt.
A teammate deletes the `if attempt == attempts - 1: raise` lines. What goes wrong when every attempt fails?

options.text: `retry` sleeps once more and then returns `None`.
options.why: Without the re-raise the last `except` falls through to `sleep`, the loop ends, and the function returns `None` as if it succeeded.
Misconception: the `for` loop runs forever. `range(attempts)` still bounds it.

options.text: Python re-raises the error after the loop.
options.why: Misconception: a caught exception is re-raised automatically. Once caught, it is gone unless re-raised.

final.explanation: The failure turns silent: the caller gets `None` and a wasted final sleep.

final.prompt: Why does `retry` re-raise after the last attempt instead of returning a default value?
final.model_answer: The caller must learn that the operation failed. A default would look like success, hide the outage, and push a wrong value further into the program.
rubric: Says the caller needs to know the call failed
Says a default value would be mistaken for a real result
Names a concrete harm, such as hiding an outage or corrupting later work
final.explanation: Met: "Returning None would look like the fetch worked and the empty value would crash later." Unmet: "Because raising is more Pythonic."
